metadata.note: Richmond, Indiana — added 2026-08-27 in answer to the observation that the map showed no passenger rail there at all. Richmond was a two-station junction town: the Pennsylvania Railroad's 1902 Daniel Burnham station on the east–west Panhandle route and the north–south line to Fort Wayne and Cincinnati, and the Chesapeake and Ohio's own station on the Cincinnati – Chicago diagonal. It was also where the Indiana and Ohio interurban networks met, which is why two traction lines are drawn here as well. Eleven features spanning 1853–1986.
metadata.why_richmond_lost_its_trains: Three separate endings. The north–south Pennsylvania service went first, with the Northern Arrow in 1961. The east–west route lasted through Penn Central to Amtrak's National Limited, which was discontinued on 1 October 1979 — the same day the Pennsylvania station closed. Amtrak's Cardinal kept calling at the ex-C&O station until it was rerouted via Connersville after 27 April 1986. Richmond has had no passenger train since.
metadata.interurban_geometry_warning: The two traction features and the Indiana Railroad features are drawn on ROAD centrelines (US 40 and US 35), not on the interurbans' own right of way. Indiana's interurban grades are essentially absent from OpenStreetMap — a sweep of abandoned, disused and razed railway along both corridors returns steam grades only. The drawn lengths match the documented ones (67.8 mi against ~68 for Indianapolis – Richmond, 42.7 against a 38-mile main line for the Dayton and Western), so the corridors are right, but the alignments are not. Each feature says so in its own geometry_quality.
metadata.national_limited_correction: data/amtrak_national_limited.geojson drew the Indianapolis – Dayton leg on the ex-New York Central through Anderson, Muncie and Union City, which misses Richmond by 39 km. The Richmond station article lists the National Limited calling here between Dayton and Indianapolis, and the station closed on 1 October 1979, the day the train was discontinued. That layer's geometry was corrected on 2026-08-27 to the ex-Pennsylvania alignment through Richmond traced for this layer.
metadata.not_drawn: Richmond's city streetcars (the Richmond Street and Interurban Railway) are not drawn: their routes were not researched, and under CLAUDE.md Rule 5 the horsecar years would have to be excluded anyway. The Indiana Railroad's post-1932 detour to Richmond by way of New Castle is not drawn — no geometry was built for the Honey Bee Route or the Dunreith – New Castle line. Nor is the Cincinnati – Chicago remainder of the C&O diagonal north of Marion, or the Pennsylvania's line north of Fort Wayne to Grand Rapids and Mackinaw City.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: (1) Every headway_min and every avg_speed_kmh in this layer is an estimate; none was read off a timetable. (2) The pre-1890 features' company names are the corporate lineage as the references give it, but no timetable or service detail was checked for 1853–1890, and the 1868 boundary between the two segments is a consolidation date rather than an observed change in service. (3) The 1871 start of the Cincinnati – Fort Wayne feature is the year the Grand Rapids and Indiana took over the Cincinnati, Richmond and Fort Wayne; when through passenger service over the whole Cincinnati – Fort Wayne route actually began was not established. (4) The exact year Richmond's C&O trains ended is given only as 'approximately 1950' by the station article. (5) Wikipedia's National Limited route map does not list Richmond even though the station article does; the station's 1 October 1979 closing date is what settles it here.

segments.note: Richmond's first train arrived in 1853, on the Indiana Central Railway building east from Indianapolis, and the town's first Union Depot followed about two decades later. East of Richmond the connection to Dayton was made by the (steam) Dayton and Western Railroad, which crossed the state line at New Paris — a separate company from the Dayton and Western Traction interurban drawn elsewhere in this layer. The station that stood here was a stop on Abraham Lincoln's funeral train in 1865, where Governor Oliver P. Morton boarded for Indianapolis. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

segments.note: Consolidated into the Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central Railway, the road that made Richmond a through point on a Columbus – Indianapolis route rather than the end of a line from Indianapolis. The Pennsylvania Railroad's Panhandle companies leased and then absorbed the property, taking the name Pittsburgh, Cincinnati, Chicago and St. Louis in 1890. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

segments.note: The Panhandle main line through Richmond, part of the Pennsylvania's New York – St. Louis and Columbus – Indianapolis routes. Richmond's Daniel Burnham-designed station of Pennsylvania granite and Indiana limestone opened in 1902 and is the centrepiece of the city's Railroad Station Historic District. headway_min of 240 stands for several through trains each way per day and is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1902 station and its architect are from the references below; the train count is not sourced.

segments.note: The named-train era at Richmond: the Spirit of St. Louis (introduced 15 June 1927, New York – St. Louis, replacing the New Yorker and the St. Louisan), the American, the Penn Texas, the Indianapolis Limited and the Union (Chicago – Columbus via Dayton) all called here. Richmond was a two-station town — these trains used the Pennsylvania station on North E Street while the Chesapeake and Ohio's trains used its own station across town. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

segments.note: Richmond's north–south railroad, and the reason the town was a junction rather than a waypoint. In June 1871 the Grand Rapids and Indiana took control of the Cincinnati, Richmond and Fort Wayne, which ran north from Richmond to Adams Junction with trackage rights on into Fort Wayne, making Richmond the southern terminus of a system that reached Grand Rapids and Mackinaw City. South of Richmond the route to Hamilton and Cincinnati was the Eaton and Hamilton and the Cincinnati, Richmond and Chicago, worked in the Pennsylvania interest. Both halves were Pennsylvania-controlled through this period, which is why the whole line carries the Pennsylvania's colour here. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the June 1871 GR&I takeover of the Cincinnati, Richmond and Fort Wayne is from the references below; the southern half's corporate detail and all service detail for this era are not sourced.

segments.note: The Pennsylvania Railroad bought the Grand Rapids and Indiana outright in 1918, making the Cincinnati – Richmond – Fort Wayne – Michigan route a single company's line. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1918 purchase is from the references below; no timetable checked.

segments.note: The Northern Arrow, Cincinnati to Mackinaw City, ran this line from 1935 to 1961, picking up connecting cars from Chicago at Fort Wayne; the Chicago – Florida Southland, which also called at Richmond, carried a Grand Rapids section over the north end until 1957. When the Northern Arrow stopped in 1961 Richmond's north–south passenger service ended with it. headway_min of 1440 is one train each way per day and is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the Northern Arrow's 1935–1961 dates and Cincinnati – Mackinaw City route, and the Southland's Grand Rapids section ending in 1957, are stated by the Fort Wayne station article; the Richmond station article lists both trains as calling here.

segments.note: Richmond's second station, and its diagonal railroad: the Cincinnati, Richmond and Muncie, incorporated in 1900 to build the shortest Cincinnati – Chicago line, renamed the Chicago, Cincinnati and Louisville in 1903, opened in stages between 1902 and 1910, and bought by the Chesapeake and Ohio in 1910 as its Chicago outlet. Into the early 1930s an unnamed C&O night train ran the whole way from Chicago to Cincinnati through Richmond and Muncie. headway_min of 1440 is one train each way per day.
sources: Segment-level: the CR&M's 1900 incorporation, 1903 renaming, 1902–1910 opening and 1910 sale to the C&O, and the Chicago – Cincinnati night train, are carried by the references below.

segments.note: From 1938 the through Chicago train was cut back to a Hammond – Cincinnati day train. C&O passenger service to Muncie ended in 1949 and Richmond's C&O station lost its trains about 1950, leaving the town with only the Pennsylvania. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the 1938 cutback and the 1949 end at Muncie are from the Muncie station article; the roughly-1950 end at Richmond is from the Richmond C&O station article, which dates the original service 'approximately 1910 to 1950'.

segments.note: Richmond got passenger trains back in 1974, at the C&O station rather than the Pennsylvania one, when Amtrak's James Whitcomb Riley began using the ex-C&O diagonal between Cincinnati and Chicago. For five years Richmond had two Amtrak stations at once — the Riley here, and the National Limited at the Pennsylvania station across town until 1979. headway_min of 1440 is one train each way per day.
sources: Segment-level: the 1974 start and the trains that served this station are listed by the Richmond C&O station article.

segments.note: The Riley was renamed the Cardinal in 1977, and the Mountaineer used the same route from 1977 to 1979. Amtrak rerouted the Cardinal after 27 April 1986 onto the ex-Baltimore and Ohio in Ohio and Indiana and the ex-Monon northwest of Indianapolis, taking it through Connersville instead: Richmond, Muncie and Marion all lost their service on that date, and Richmond has had no passenger train since. headway_min is one train each way per day.
sources: Segment-level: the 27 April 1986 last day at Richmond, the renaming, the Mountaineer's 1977–1979 dates and the reroute via Connersville onto the ex-B&O and ex-Monon are from the references below.

properties.company: Terre Haute, Indianapolis and Eastern Traction Company
properties.line: Terre Haute, Indianapolis & Eastern: Indianapolis – Richmond
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE, not sourced. 45 km/h (28 mph) is a typical interurban limited's end-to-end average over 68 miles with street running at both ends; no schedule was consulted.
properties.geometry_quality: NOT the interurban's own right of way. Indiana's interurban grades are essentially absent from OpenStreetMap, so this line is drawn on the centreline of US 40 — the National Road — which the cars ran beside for most of the route, through the same towns in the same order (Cumberland, Greenfield, Charlottesville, Knightstown, Dunreith, Lewisville, Cambridge City, Centerville). The Indianapolis end follows Washington Street from the Traction Terminal out to Irvington, which is where the first section opened in 1900. Drawn length 67.8 mi against a documented ~68, which says the corridor is right; individual curves, private right of way stretches and the Richmond approach are not. Where the cars ran on their own graded right of way beside the road this will be off by a few hundred metres.

segments.note: Built piecemeal between 1900 and 1903 — the first section, Irvington to Greenfield, opened 13 June 1900 — with a trial car running the whole way from Indianapolis to Richmond on 5 June 1903. Buffet and parlor car service began in January 1905, with connections at Richmond onto the Ohio interurban network for Dayton and Columbus. Drawn from 1903, the year of through service, not from the 1900 first section. headway_min of 60 is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the 1900–1903 construction, the 13 June 1900 first section, the 5 June 1903 trial car and the January 1905 parlor service are from the line's own article.

segments.note: Operated by the Terre Haute, Indianapolis and Eastern Traction Company from 1907. By 1924 seven limited trains ran each day between Indianapolis and Richmond, the eastbound ones named the Buckeye Express and the westbound the Hoosier Express. The Milton branch was given up on 20 December 1925. headway_min of 60 is an ESTIMATE — the seven limiteds were on top of the local cars.
sources: Segment-level: the THI&E's 1907–1931 operation, the 1924 count of seven limiteds, the two train names and the 20 December 1925 Milton branch closure are from the line's own article.

segments.note: The line passed to the consolidated Indiana Railroad in 1931. It ran the full Indianapolis – Richmond route for only a few months: from January 1932 the Indianapolis – Dunreith section was abandoned and Richmond cars were sent instead by way of New Castle, over the ex-Union Traction Honey Bee Route and the Dunreith – New Castle line. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

segments.note: What was left after January 1932: the Dunreith – Cambridge City – Richmond end of the line, reached from Indianapolis by a detour through New Castle that is NOT drawn here because the map has no geometry for the Honey Bee Route or the Dunreith – New Castle line. Rising costs and the loss of interchange traffic with the Cincinnati and Lake Erie finished it; the final cars ran on 9 May 1937, the same day the Dayton and Western quit at the other end of town. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE, not sourced. 38 km/h (24 mph) is a guess at a 38-mile interurban with street running at both ends.
properties.geometry_quality: NOT the interurban's own right of way, for the same reason as the Indianapolis line: drawn on the US 35 road corridor between Richmond and Dayton, plus Main Street through Richmond. Worse than the US 40 trace in one specific way — west of Dayton US 35 is now a limited-access expressway on a modern alignment, so that stretch is a corridor, not a route. Drawn 42.7 mi against a documented 38-mile main line; the excess is the 5 mi of Richmond city streets at the west end plus the expressway's own geometry.

segments.note: The Dayton and Western began running Dayton west to Eaton on 26 June 1898 and completed its line into Richmond on 24 July 1903, serving New Lebanon, Johnsville, West Alexandria, Eaton, New Hope and New Westville along the way. It was the most direct connection between the Ohio and Indiana interurban networks — with the Indianapolis line at Richmond it formed part of a continuous electric route from Terre Haute to Zanesville. Leased by the Ohio Electric interests from 1903 and part of the Ohio Electric Railway system from 1907. Drawn from 1903, the year the through line opened; the 1898 Dayton – Eaton section is not drawn separately. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the 26 June 1898 opening to Eaton, the 24 July 1903 completion to Richmond, the town list and the Ohio Electric lease are from the company's own article.

segments.note: Independent again from 25 April 1920, and bankrupt by 1931. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the 25 April 1920 return to independent operation and the 1931 bankruptcy are from the company's own article.

segments.note: After the 1931 bankruptcy the line was run by the Cincinnati and Lake Erie, the Ohio system whose high-speed cars are the ones usually remembered from this network. It sold the property to a trust company in 1936. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.

segments.note: The last nine months were run under lease by the Indiana Railroad, which ended service on 9 May 1937 — the same day it dropped the Indianapolis line into Richmond from the other direction. The colour here stays the Cincinnati and Lake Erie's rather than splitting a nine-month lease into its own feature; the operator is named in this note instead. Losing the Dayton and Western helped finish the C&LE, which collapsed two years later. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the Indiana Railroad's nine-month lease, the 9 May 1937 last run and the effect on the C&LE are from the Dayton and Western article.
